question.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by 

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2n+1}}{n}.
$$

Find ${a}_{n},$ given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.
$$

current_example.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=3$ is given by

$$
\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{ (x-3)^{n}}{n}
$$

Find $a_n,$ given that

$$
f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n.
$$
current_example.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217743/assets/37873acadee9b506df2227f7875450947870bb9f755188b4ff9c65384195a609.svg)

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217743/assets/f0f00a211bba8674413a5d0300e7adfe6761b83083d573f53bdcc594487978c6.svg)
We can now write the Taylor series for $f'(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty (x-3)^{n-1}.
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
a_n = (x-3)^{n-1}.
$$
